extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and procedural rules governing cancellation/repeal of patents — both between rival patentees (interferences/annulments) and in the public interest — as derived from statutes, common law, and leading case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of repeal (whole or partial)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgment of repeal may embrace the whole patent, ... or may include only the particular inventions which are covered by the rival patent and are found by the court to have been first invented by the rival patentee. Both patents are equally before the court for judgment and either may be repealed ... to any extent which may be necessary in order to secure to the party claiming under the prior inventor ... the unqualified enjoyment of the monopoly to which he is entitled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may cancel an entire patent when the adversary's inventive genius produced the entire patentable subject-matter, or may cancel only those claims/inventions that conflict; remedies are tailored to secure the prior inventor's effective monopoly. (Cites: various interference/annulment cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues in annulment under Sec. 4918 (interference petitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this proceeding the patentability of the inventions described and claimed in the antagonistic patents is not in issue. Priority of invention is the only point in controversy, and judgment, therefore, is awarded to the party who derives his title from the first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annulment petitions under Sec. 4918 focus on priority/interference; courts will not relitigate patentability. (See Sawyer v. Massey and other cited authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office decisions not binding in court annulment proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: That in proceedings to annul under Sec. 4918, the courts are not bound by the decisions of the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the Patent Office previously allowed or rejected claims, courts handling annulment/interference suits may reach their own conclusions. (Cites: Holliday v. Pickhardt; Asbestos Felting Co. v. Salamander Felting Co.; Minneapolis Harvester Works v. McCormick Harvesting Mach. Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-ordered delivery and cancellation under Sec. 58 (act of 1870)
rubrics_metrics.description: That under Sec. 58, act of 1870, the court may order the defeated patent to be delivered to the clerk and cancelled by him, and sent to the Secretary of the Interior with a copy of the decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When decree to annul is entered, the court has statutory authority (Sec. 58, 1870) to direct ministerial cancellation and transmission of the patent record to executive branch officials. (See Sturges v. Van Hagen.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions after annulment and limits on preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: That where the court annuls a patent it may enjoin the patentee from instituting actions thereon. That a junior patentee cannot be enjoined from suing under his patent on the motion of the prior patentee, pending a suit by the prior patentee to cancel the junior patent, when the patentability of the inventions described and claimed in the antagonistic patents is not in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent is finally annulled, courts can enjoin suits based on it. But prior patentees cannot obtain preliminary injunctions to stop a junior patentee from suing if patentability is not contested in the cancellation action; equitable relief is constrained by the limited issues in the annulment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on defenses in petitions to annul under Sec. 4918
rubrics_metrics.description: That on proceedings for repeal under Sec. 4918, a plea that the plaintiff's patent is void for want of novelty is improper; the defendant cannot set up by pleas a defence, if holding under a later patent, that the invention was in use before the plaintiff's inventive act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural limits exist on the matters defendants may plead in an annulment petition based on interference/priority; certain defenses (e.g., novelty challenges) are inappropriate in that special procedural posture. (See Pentlaige v. Pentlarge and related citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of abandonment of experiments followed by later patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: That on a petition to annul, if it appears that one patentee abandoned his experiments, and after the issue of a patent to his rival renewed them and patented the invention, the rival patent will be sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment of development followed by later re‑execution and patenting can preclude a cancellation claim based on priority; courts examine claimant's continuous pursuit and abandonment facts. (See Hutchinson v. Everett.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may institute repeal in the public interest (historical/private vs public remedies)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proceeding under the acts of 1790 and 1798 afforded a private, not a public, remedy: the proceeding was to be instituted by a private person who was to be liable for the costs if his effort failed. The general public is left to the protection of the government and its officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early statutes allowed individuals to bring repeal actions (subject to costs/limitations); absence or repeal of those statutory procedures does not necessarily prove the government lacks any equitable remedy, but historically the statutory remedy was a private action (scire facias style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-law grounds for revocation of sovereign grants (three classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law a grant by the sovereign was revocable in three classes of cases: (1) Where the same subject-matter had been previously granted; (2) Where the grant had been procured by fraud; (3) Where the subject-matter of the grant could not legally be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three classical categories supply the common-law foundation for rescission/repeal of patents in the public interest; courts apply them when relevant in equity actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court conclusions on statutory vs inherent remedies (U.S. v. American Bell summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summed up conclusions from United States v. American Bell Telephone Co.: (1) All rights and remedies of patentees arise out of the Constitution and the acts of Congress, and where these are silent no right or remedy exists. (2) The power to cancel a patent is not embraced among general equity powers — the patent rests wholly on statute. (3) A bill to cancel a patent cannot be maintained in the name of the United States in the absence of an express statute to that effect. (4) The power to cancel a land patent does not extend to patents for inventions, since the government grants land but not the invention. (5) Under the acts of 1790 and 1793 a patent could be cancelled on scire facias if surreptitiously obtained, but under later acts this is a ground of defence in infringement suits only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are treated as the Court's principal holdings and are relied upon to delimit the role of statute, equity, and the sovereign in patent-cancellation matters; the text discusses and critiques each conclusion and their implications for public‑interest repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government's sovereign power to rescind unlawful patents (equity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States has power to repeal unlawful patents, irrespective of any special provision of the Constitution to that effect, or any act of Congress conferring that authority, but solely as a part of its sovereignty; the government may proceed in equity to interfere for the rescission of a monopoly unlawfully obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise argues that where public property or public rights are injured by a fraudulently obtained patent, sovereign power and equitable principles support government action to annul or rescind the patent even absent explicit statutory repeal procedure; cites cases (United States v. Gunning; Attorney‑General v. Rumford Chemical Works) and analyzes analogies to land grants and franchises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy limited to parties (res judicata and scope of decree)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decree of repeal may be of no validity except between the parties to the suit; the general public is left to the protection of the government and its officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When individuals obtain decrees in private repeal proceedings, the effect is generally inter partes; for broader public protection, government-initiated or statutory remedies may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive principle: statutes do not extinguish common-law/equity rights unless explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: As in every other instance where express legislation relates to subject-matter already known to the common law, the statute does not exclude what it does not mention or impliedly repeal, but both the written and unwritten law must be construed together and taken as the measure of the rights and remedies with which they deal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should construe patent statutes alongside existing common-law/equitable doctrines; absence of a statute expressly providing a remedy is not necessarily conclusive that no remedy exists, although the Supreme Court has sometimes framed the issue otherwise.
